[0.1] The Halcyon storage engine keeps every table as an append-only sequence of immutable segments. A write is first appended to the write-ahead log on the primary device, then buffered in a memtable held in host memory. When the memtable reaches the configured threshold the writer seals it, hands it to the background flusher, and starts a new memtable without blocking readers, so a segment on disk is always complete and never mutated in place.

[0.2] Compaction merges segments that overlap in key range. Halcyon distinguishes two triggers. The size trigger fires when a level holds more bytes than its tier budget allows, and it merges the whole level into the next tier. The debt trigger fires when a segment has been read more often than it has been rewritten, and it merges only the hottest segments of that level, which keeps read amplification bounded while leaving cold data untouched for long periods.

[0.3] Each segment carries a header with its key range, a Bloom filter, a block index and a checksum per block. The Bloom filter is sized from the segment's key count at seal time and is never resized. When a segment is queried and the filter reports a false positive, the reader pays one block read; the filter's saturation is tracked per segment, and a saturated filter is recorded in the manifest so the next compaction pass knows that the segment's read cost has drifted upward.

[0.4] Readers never take a lock that a writer holds. A query pins a manifest version, resolves the segment set from it, and then reads blocks through a page cache keyed by segment identifier and block offset. Because segments are immutable, a pinned manifest keeps its data alive even while compaction is replacing the segments underneath it; the old files are unlinked only when the last reader that pinned them moves on.

[0.5] The write-ahead log is truncated in whole files, not in the middle. Every flush records the log sequence number of the last record it persisted, and a log file becomes eligible for deletion once a flushed segment covers every record it contains. On recovery Halcyon replays the surviving log files in order and stops at the first record whose checksum fails, treating the remainder of that file as a torn tail that a crash interrupted and that the writer had not yet acknowledged.

[0.6] Memory during compaction is bounded by one knob: the maximum bytes a merge stage may buffer. A merge reads its inputs with a fixed-size window, writes output blocks of a fixed size, and spills the pending output when the budget is exhausted. The budget therefore trades compaction throughput against resident memory without changing the shape of the output segments, which is why it is the only memory knob the engine exposes to operators.
